column1: For the past three years, I have lived in Ukraine with my wife, both of us working for humanitarian organizations. We moved there after the Russian invasion began in 2022, and a few months ago we returned to Spain. Upon returning to the EU, I clearly felt a widespread lack of understanding and concern for the issue of Ukraine, the reality and consequences of the war, Europe's role and responsibility in this war, and the lives of the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian refugees in Europe. Aside from a few exceptions and specific contexts, I find it difficult to understand—and partly accept—this low level of engagement, information, and activity, even indirect or merely emotional, of so many people in the place where I live. I also find the response and determination of most European institutions in seeking a solution utterly inadequate.

In other words, there is a lack of culture and awareness, and widespread shortsightedness regarding workplace safety and health.

She voted Volt for the national election, she is progressive, keeps up (from a distance) with geopolitical events, is social etc. However, in the days of the election and afterwards, she saw a bunch of small videos on social media, after which I had (for me) a very weird, alienating conversation with her. She said that she saw Geert Wilders (ultranationalist) on Nieuwsuur (serious intellectual tv show) and that she thought he was a very reasonable guy, that she was happy that he would finally take the drama out of political debate, and just sit down with people and FINALLY come up with solutions for the country. Turns out she saw some very smartly cut out (populist) videos, and she never really heard any speeches from the guy. It is like history of the last 20 years of hateful speeches was just completely not there anymore. To me this was a very alienating feeling, trying to tell her what this guys ideology actually is, but I could not convince her... I've had more of these conversations with different people and it feels disappointing that even very smart, nuanced people are falling for the cleverly layed out populist arguments.

column1:
I am a woman, born woman, and I have been in therapy for almost 2 years. Because my father, a conservative man, psychologically abused my mother and me for our gender, and finances were one of his bigger weapons. 
He, aside from more pshycologically based abuses, like conditional love or strictness and control and isolating us, convinced my mother women could not handle money, a belief that was then passed to me. "The man handles the money. Women are bad with money". He would spend my mothers money, when she earned more than him. But not let her learn about or do taxes on her own. He would choose insurances, banks to open accounts in, investments, without consulting her, and always said and assumed that, until I was married, he could just do the same with me. 

I still have anxiety attacks when I do expensive purchases or handle my IRS, I also have panic attacks when I start searching for house loans or ways to invest in real state, so I can buy a house. Because it was induced in me this idea of "if you try, it will go wrong, you will loose all your money and live in the streets". Something he would repeat often. 

Did you know that there are cases of financial bullying, coersion, coerced debt, damaged credit scores, and deep correlations between womens lack of financial literacy and the amount of time women will stay in abusive relationships? The data exists. 

One of the reasons I cannot trust the far-left on this topic, is that leftist forces, like portuguese party Bloco de Esquerda (left block) have correlated financial literacy as a capitalist trap that makes people do bad decisions, almost calling it a "liberal" conspiracy to promote capitalist think tanks and ideas. How can a party that is supposedly pro social-justice ever present themselves as feminist and pro working class defend such a statement? On the other side of the spectrum, conservative political groups just want the women to return to more traditional roles, leaving these situations more open to become the norm. 

If you are truly a feminist, you will defend  the hability of women to financially protect themselves from any kind of financial abuse. Not shame them from engaging in this type of education, for the sake of protecting a supposed anti-capitalist utopia you have as a goal to construct. If not for ideological reasons, do it for pragmatic ones. The anti-capitalist utopia will not come in our lifetime, if ever, but there are women being convinced they are financially unstable and abused by the men in their lives right now. And not just women, anyone with lack of financial literacy is more prone to make bad decision with their money. Not everyone can precisely throw their money at a personal assistant or consultant to gain or not loose money. And leaves them more vulnerable to any miracle worker that tells them how to get rich quick. If you truly are for feminism, you will teach them to have a positive relationship with money and teach them how to handle it alone. 

This is where Volt can make a difference. Differenciate from other parties that fall under this trap. Don't run away from the idea that money and grow personal wealth can be a positive thing. And pass the message that women can do it as well as men. Not for the purpose of getting rich, but for the purpose of being free from an actual form of patriarchy.

column1: Over the course of the last 11 months, I've been part of a group of Muslims and Jews in German-speaking Switzerland that come together to share feelings and thoughts about the "Israeli-Palestinian conflict". Our goal is to create a safe space of understanding that offers room for diverging feelings and narratives - in a time when there are few spaces where people feel like they can share their fear, anger, despair, and hope openly - without being misunderstood or attacked. The group is an attempt to not let our communities in Switzerland be drawn into division in the face of all the unspeakable violence in Israel, Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon. This groups is one of the few places where I feel I can breathe. Where there is room for the complexity of lives, narratives, collective identities. And mostly pain. There is so much pain that festers in people as long as they cannot share it and as long as they feel they aren't seen. Every meeting we've had is a small universe in itself. Calm, deep, sad, and hopeful. After each meeting I leave the room both heavier and lighter. Heavier as I start to understand more perspectives on the unspeakable violence and suffering. Lighter as I see that there are wonderful people dedicated to coming tother and emphasising the holiness of life and solidarity to each others' humanity - without forgetting their particular identities.

When I was young, I had many ideals.

Back in the 80s, we were afraid that someone would push the wrong button and our civilization would be wiped out in a nuclear war.

We had acid rain, a hole in the ozone layer, and the idea of ​​planting an apple tree could be considered the ultimate in optimism...

Then came the change in Eastern Europe. "Walking through the park... on Scorpions" perfectly captured that hope. It was on the radio while I was visiting a factory in Gdansk, whose continued existence I then worked on as a Western European marketing expert. The factory still exists today.

I returned after a few years, wanting to balance family and career. Now, 30 years later, I'm actually still happily married; my son is doing his master's degree, and I'm a department head at work. I have a house in a good location, with photovoltaic panels, and my electric car runs on its own electricity from the roof.
Yes, I'm probably a winner. But it wasn't/isn't easy. And the efforts have left their mark. Little remains of the former idealism. Digitalization seemed to be the key to greater participation, a sharing economy, and knowledge for all. Today, tech billionaires control "the masses" via social media. Ironically, by convincing them that being against it means freedom...
So what can we do? Survive ourselves, protect our own interests, and not give up completely, even if it's just to subscribe to the VOLT newsletter.

I find the development of public discourse on divisive topics in our European societies increasingly disturbing and very dangerous: whether the topic may be migration, Israel/Palestine, or 'woke' topics related to civil liberties (LGBTQ; - the public discourse is very polarised, and increasingly hostile, and coercive. This is very present in public (at demonstrations, counter-demonstrations), publicly held debates,social media platforms, and also mainstream media, and even universities.  People holding different or more nuanced perspectives on such issues are increasingly vilified or attempted to be silenced, and increasingly overtly. Contentious issues are presented in increasingly binary ways ('for', 'against'; and adding defamatory labels on the 'other', aiming to delegitimize and increasingly dehumanise others holding different opinions or positions. 
Regardless of the specific issue where this manifests, this tendency is a very dangerous development for our democratic societies, leading to ever-increasing polarisation and radicalisation, and incitement to hate and violence, and terrorism, and a breakdown of democratic values and societies. 

In such a climate, it is becoming very difficult for individuals to voice different perspectives and different world-views in public (and often even within personal networks), whether off-line or online. In many contexts (workplace settings), discourse about such issues is therefore often avoided, to prevent the outbreak of conflicts. 

In my view, we urgently need spaces and processes that allow the expression of 'minority views' and dissenting voices, in line with democratic values (free speech, expression of values), whilst always staying respectful of other peoples' different views. In the spirit of this quote: 

"“I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.”
― S.G. Tallentyre, The Friends of Voltaire"

or this: 
"“If liberty means anything at all, it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.”
― George Orwell"

It was during the lunch break when my colleague and I were sitting opposite each other, each with a Tupperware container, as usual. The topic of conversation was clear. We had to talk about what had happened a few hours earlier. We both witnessed our dear colleague from Ukraine sitting at her desk, tears streaming down her face. We listened to her. We heard how her immediate family experienced the war. These are images that, without us having experienced them ourselves, etched themselves in our minds. The death of a former schoolmate at the front—he was very bright, smart, and perhaps only twenty-five. I remember the postcard from my great-uncle. "Finally, it's starting. We're heading for Father's homeland," it says, handwritten on the back. The front shows him as a soldier. Three days later, he was shot at the front.

But my colleague is no longer crying for her former schoolmate. Nor for her father and brother, who are scheduled to be drafted towards the end of the year. She's crying because her husband, the father of her son, is also facing deportation from Germany, and his ID card can only be renewed in Ukraine. If he goes back to Ukraine, what will happen? If Merz and many other politicians here in the country have their way, then men abroad should defend their homeland.

"Would you defend your homeland?" I ask my colleague. "Yes, after all, it's about democratic values, about our freedom," is his reply. "But what if you were to lose your life for it, your only life?" - "Yes, because I can protect the lives of others for it," he tells me. I say to him: "I think you're too far away from the war, and it seems like a game to you." He is outraged and tells me that the war is in Europe and not far away at all – a politician or a journalist could have said something similar.

I say to him, not because I know, but because I suspect it: "When you see someone dying and everything around you is terrible, then you might ask yourself why you have to sacrifice your life for this war. Who are you really sacrificing yourself for?" I shake my head and conclude by saying: "Are you familiar with Albert Schweitzer and his work *Reverence for Life*?" He says no, and I begin to understand that he can probably be a pawn, like my great-uncle, fueling everything.

Es war in der Mittagspause, als mein Kollege und ich wie gewöhnlich jeweils mit Tupperdose gegenüber saßen. Das Gesprächsthema war klar. Wir mussten über das, was ein paar Stunden vorher passiert war, sprechen. Wir beide hatten mitbekommen, wie unsere liebe Kollegin aus der Ukraine mit Tränen am Schreibtisch saß. Wir haben ihr zugehört. Wir haben gehört, wie ihre nächste Familie den Krieg erlebt. Es sind Bilder, die, ohne dass wir sie selbst erlebt haben, sich in den Gedanken verkrallen. Der Tod eines ehemaligen Schulkameraden an der Front – er war sehr aufgeweckt, schlau und vielleicht erst fünfundzwanzig. Ich erinnere mich an die Postkarte meines Urgroßonkels. „Endlich geht’s los. Es geht Richtung Vaters Heimat“, steht handgeschrieben auf der Rückseite. Die Vorderseite zeigt ihn als Soldat. Drei Tage später wird er an der Front erschossen.

Aber meine Kollegin weint nicht mehr um ihren ehemaligen Schulkameraden. Auch nicht um ihren Vater und Bruder, die gegen Ende des Jahres eingezogen werden sollen. Sie weint, weil auch ihrem Mann und Vater ihres Sohnes die Ausweisung aus Deutschland droht und die Erneuerung des Ausweises nur noch in der Ukraine möglich ist. Wenn er zurück in die Ukraine geht, was passiert dann? Wenn es nach Merz und vielen anderen Politikern hier im Lande geht, dann sollten die Männer im Ausland ihr Vaterland verteidigen.

„Würdest du dein Vaterland verteidigen?“, frage ich meinen Kollegen. „Ja, es geht ja schließlich um die demokratischen Werte, um unsere Freiheit“, lautet seine Antwort. „Aber wenn du dafür dein Leben verlieren würdest, dein einziges Leben?“ – „Ja, weil ich dafür das Leben der anderen schützen kann“, lässt er mich wissen. Ich sage zu ihm: „Ich glaube, du bist zu weit weg vom Krieg, und es scheint für dich wie ein Spiel.“ Er ist empört und lässt mich wissen, dass der Krieg doch in Europa sei und gar nicht weit weg – es hätte so oder so ähnlich auch ein Politiker oder ein Journalist sagen können.

Ich sage zu ihm, nicht weil ich es weiß, sondern weil ich es vermute: „Wenn du jemanden sterben siehst und es um dich herum schrecklich ist, dann fragst du dich vielleicht, warum es sein muss, dass du für diesen Krieg dein Leben opferst. Für wen opferst du dich eigentlich wirklich?“ Ich schüttle den Kopf und sage zum Abschluss: „Kennst du Albert Schweitzer und sein Werk Die Ehrfurcht vor dem Leben?“ Er verneint, und ich beginne zu verstehen, dass er wohl wie mein Urgroßonkel eine Spielfigur sein kann und alles befeuert.

column1:
Dennis or Deniz?
My brother's neighbor is of Turkish origin, married a woman, and took her last name.
When he sent me his contact information, he read "Dennis *Last Name*" and his wife looked over it, commenting, "Nicely written in German."
My reaction *confused, questioning face*. The answer is Deniz (a surname of Turkish origin that translates as "goatherder").

The one important question that arises for me:

Why is the MALE first name "Deniz" in Turkish, a gender-neutral first name in German, and its 'German' variant, "Dennis," is masculine?!
Should I now inform my esteemed friend and tell him to officially change his name at the registry office, otherwise he'll still be considered a gender-neutral person? That would be horrible.

Joking aside.

The self-determination law, as it exists in Germany, has always been more progressive. I'm so incredibly happy that I can FINALLY legally decide on my gender identification *self-determined* (still subject to certain conditions). For that, I thank the traffic light coalition! (or rather, the Greens and SPD).

Personal success: As of April 24, 2025, my gender identity is legally valid and my name change is sealed. Almost a kind of birthday success, four days before mine.

This success, or rather the motivation that arises from it, to support others in the future to pursue this path to the freedom of self-determination of their own first name and gender, AND to pave the way for the future by incorporating a nationwide and subsequently Europe-wide roadmap.

Wieso ist im Türkischen der MÄNNLICHE Vorname "Deniz", im Deutschen ein geschlechtsneutraler Vorname & seine 'deutsche' Variante "Dennis" männlich?!

A year ago, my daughter was born with apert syndrome. In most cases, the syndrome is not diagnosed until birth. We were fortunate that my wife changed gynecologists two months before the delivery, and she recognized the syndrome immediately. The doctors at the university hospital where my wife gave birth didn't have time to thoroughly examine our situation beforehand, which is why they initially talked about a natural birth and only decided on a cesarean section one day before the due date. After the birth, the university hospital performed several tests, many of which resulted in incorrect diagnoses (deafness, cataracts, very early operations to separate bones, etc.). We had contacted the parents' initiative for apert children beforehand, which informed us that we would need to go to specialized clinics for examinations.
Thirteen days after the birth, we discharged our daughter from the university hospital against medical advice (we were pressured not to do this) and traveled from Schleswig-Holstein to Würzburg to a specialized clinic. All examinations were repeated there, and we were able to return home after three days. We had a schedule of which treatments and surgeries our daughter would need, when, and which clinics we would need to go to.
The parents from the parents' initiative confirmed to us that in almost all cases, the maternity clinics try to carry out further treatment in-house and do not refer the patient to a specialized clinic. How can we prevent non-specialist clinics from using their limited resources to treat "exciting medical cases" themselves?

Wir hatten das Glück, dass meine Frau zwei Monate vor der Entbindung die Frauenärztin gewechselt hat, welche das Syndrom sofort erkannte. Die Ärzte in der Uni-Klinik, in welcher meine Frau entbunden hat, hatte keine Zeit sich mit unserer Situation vorab intensiver auseinander zu setzen, weswegen vorab noch von einer spontanen Geburt gesprochen wurde und sich erst einen Tag vor dem Entbindungstermin von seitens der Ärzte für einen Kaiserschnitt entschieden wurde. Nach der Geburt wurden von der Uniklinik mehrere Tests gemacht, welche zum großteil Fehldiagnosen beinhalteten (taub, grauer starr, sehr frühe Operationen zum trennen von Knochen...). column1:
After the results of last year's European elections, I was devastated. How can that be?! Afterward, I clearly felt the need to do something to promote understanding, to get people talking to each other again instead of exposing themselves to polarization and projections. Together, we developed a format to make democracy tangible on a small scale through dialogue, listening, encounters, a "safe" space, to get to the essence and the people behind the opinions.

We've since held a few such events. Each time, different people came, some came more often, and not just from the "activist/change bubble." And each time, they left with more vitality, a smile, and lively conversation with new people they'd met. Some thanked us personally and asked if something like this could happen more often.

Yes, it can, and that's what makes democracy fun! But it requires much more funding (we were fortunate enough to receive funding through a small partnership to at least partially compensate for our efforts). And it takes training and empowerment to empower many more people to moderate/host dialogue and similar formats.
Last week, we experienced the US elections and the collapse of our traffic light government. This reminds me again how important such spaces are for strengthening democracy. It makes sense, requires a lot of energy (citizens are exhausting ;) because they're heterogeneous, etc.), and is incredibly meaningful and important.

I'm not alone in my commitment. It's empowering. But unfortunately, many people share the exhaustion, the personal discrimination, and the loss of friendships when you stand up for democracy.

Danach keimte deutlich in mir auf, etwas zur Verständigung zu tun, dass die Menschen wieder miteinander reden statt sich Polarisierungen und Projektionen auszusetzen. Gemeinsam haben wir ein Format entwickelt, Demokratie im Kleinen erlebbar zu machen durch Dialog, Zuhören, Begegnung, einen "Sicheren" Raum, zur Essenz und den Menschen hinter der Meinung zu finden. 
Inzwischen haben wir ein paar solcher Veranstaltungen durchgeführt. Jedes Mal kamen andere Menschen, einige kamen öfters, nicht nur aus der "Aktivisten/Wandel-Blase". Und jedes Mal gingen sie mit mehr Lebendigkeit, einem Lächeln und im regen Gespräch mit Neu-Kennengelernten wieder nach Hause. Einige haben sich persönlich bei uns bedankt und gebeten, ob sowas nicht öfters stattfinden kann. 
Ja, das kann es und so macht Demokratie Spaß! Doch braucht es dafür viel mehr Mittel (wir hatten das Glück, durch eine kleine Kooperation Fördermittel zu bekommen, um unseren Aufwand wenigstens ehwas bezahlt zu bekommen). Und es braucht Befähigung/Trainings, um viel mehr Menschen zu befähigen, Dialog- u.ä. Formate zu moderieren/hosten.
Vergangene Woche haben wir die US-Wahlen und den Bruch unserer Ampelregierung erlebt. Wieder regt das in mir an, wie wichtig solche Räume sind zur Stärkung der Demokratie. Das macht Sinn, braucht viel Energie (Bürger*innen sind anstrengend ;) weil inhomogen etc.) und ist ungaublich sinnvoll und wichtig. 

Mit meinem Engagement bin ich nicht allein. Das bestärkt. Doch teilen leider auch viele Menschen die Erschöpfung, die persönliche Diskriminierung und verlieren Freundschaften, wenn man sich für Demokratie einsetzt.

column1:
I repeatedly observe that public institutions, whether administrative or educational, do not truly support inclusion. The UNCRPD has been ratified, but everything that needs to be changed is perceived as an imposition by many people in our society. This inner attitude, which no one – except the AfD – articulates out loud, leads to people only pretending to do something for marginalized groups. In reality, nothing changes. This widespread tokenism is a disgrace because so much money is wasted without achieving anything.

Yet there are still far too many violations of human rights and physical integrity in marginalized communities.

It is simply unbelievable what, for example, is currently being done to children born deaf in wealthy Western countries. In medicine, the cochlear implant was invented, and now it is implanted in a major, expensive operation in every baby diagnosed as profoundly hard of hearing or deaf shortly after birth. A lot of money is at stake, and the clinics make a lot of money from it. It's completely unclear whether these children benefit at all. And what's even worse: parents have stopped communicating with their children using sign language under pressure from doctors. This currently leads to what is known as language-induced intellectual disability in the children, because they receive too little language input and their language-related cognitive system cannot develop. If the child then doesn't develop as desired—which, by the way, the first stage has nothing to do with and doesn't take responsibility for—some invalid diagnostic instruments are used, and the children, who are actually just deaf and would develop cognitively normally with sign language, are then diagnosed with "mental disability." This is how the children end up in special schools for people with learning difficulties, where they no longer receive any sign language input at all, and the input from the CI is deficient on a spoken language level. This means that healthy, normal children who would have experienced normal cognitive development with sign language suffer irreparable cognitive neurological damage as a result of this practice. They later end up in institutional care or psychiatric hospitals.

It is not only outrageous, but simply scandalous, that there is currently an epidemic of language deprivation. The World Federation of the Deaf (https://signhealth.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/2022-Position-paper-on-access-to-national-sign-languages-as-a-health-need-World-Federation-of-the-Deaf.pdf) and the National Association of the Deaf (https://www.nad.org/language-deprivation/) have long pointed this out. Deaf people are not being heard, even though they should have a voice.

Ich stelle immer wieder fest, dass öffentliche Institutionen, seien es Verwaltung oder Bildungsinstitutionen, Inklusion nicht wirklich unterstützen. Die UN-BRK wurde ratifiziert, aber alles, was verändert werden muss, wird von vielen Menschen in unserer Gesellschaft als Zumutung empfunden. Diese innere Haltung, die keiner – außer der AfD - laut artikuliert– führt dazu, dass nur so getan wird, als ob man etwas für marginalisierte Gruppen tut. In Wahrheit ändert sich nichts. Dieser weit verbreitete Tokenismus ist eine Schande, weil so unheimlich viel Geld verschwendet wird, ohne dass etwas dabei herumkommt. 

Dabei gibt es noch immer viel zu viele Verstöße gegen die Menschenrechte und die körperliche Unversehrtheit in marginalisierten Communitys. 

Es ist schlicht unglaublich, was beispielsweise derzeit taub geborenen Kindern in den westlichen reichen Ländern angetan wird. In der Medizin hat man das Cochlea-Implantat erfunden und nun wird es jedem Baby, das kurz nach der Geburt als hochgradig schwerhörig oder taub diagnostiziert wird, in einer großen, teuren OP eingepflanzt. Da geht es um viel Geld, und die Kliniken verdienen gut daran. Es ist völlig unklar, ob diese Kinder überhaupt davon profitieren. Und was noch viel schlimmer ist: Eltern haben auf Druck der Ärzte aufgehört, mit ihren Kindern gebärdensprachlich zu kommunizieren. Das führt aktuell zu einer sogenannten sprachlich induzierten geistigen Behinderung bei den Kindern, weil sie zu wenig sprachlichen Input bekommen und ihr sprachliches, kognitives System sich nicht entfalten kann. Wenn das Kind sich dann nicht so entwickelt, wie gewünscht, womit die erste übrigens dann nichts mehr zu tun haben und dafür auch keine Verantwortung übernehmen, werden irgendwelche nicht validen Diagnostik-Instrumente herangezogen und die Kinder, die eigentlich nur taub sind, und sich mit Gebärdensprache kognitiv ganz normal entwickeln würden, bekommen dann die Diagnose "geistig behindert". So landen die Kinder in Förderschulen für Menschen mit Lernschwierigkeiten, wo sie gar keinen gebärdensprachlichen Input mehr bekommen und der Input mit dem CI auf lautsprachlicher Ebene defizitär ist. Das bedeutet, dass gesunde normale Kinder, die mit einer Gebärdensprache eine normale kognitive Entwicklung genommen hätten, durch diese Praxis einen kognitiven neurologischen Schaden erleiden, der niemals wieder gutzumachen ist. Sie landen später in Heimen oder in der Psychiatrie.
Es ist nicht nur empörend, sondern einfach skandalös, dass es aktuell zu einer Epidemie der Sprachdeprivation kommt. Darauf weist die "World Federation of the Deaf" ( https://signhealth.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/2022-Position-paper-on-access-to-national-sign-languages-as-a-health-need-World-Federation-of-the-Deaf.pdf )und die 'National Association of the Deaf' ( https://www.nad.org/language-deprivation/ )schon lange hin. Taube Menschen werden nicht gehört, obwohl sie eine Stimme haben sollten.

column1: As a woman of 60 who built a career in IT and worked her way honestly to leadership level, I moved to Netherlands, and find that I am not taken seriously when applying for a senior role. And yet, I have been unemployed over a year, have experienced a great deal of sexism from male hiring managers and male CEO's as interviewers. I note, no women in the process other than the secretary, and I hear statements of bias that are cringeworthy. And I hear those statements alone, which adds to my streee.   When Dutch companies want a seasoned expert on their board or running their department, they find they have confidence in a man, regardless of skills, experience, or seniority, and declare that they hire the "best & brightest regardless of gender". column1:
I suspect I have ASD (autism spectrum disorder). This suspicion was confirmed by an autism counseling center. However, the official diagnosis must be made by a psychiatrist. The problem: No one in the psychiatric field I can reach can treat/diagnose me because they are not familiar with it. Specialists and therapists are overworked because health insurance companies aren't issuing new practice permits, meaning there are too few therapists. Consequently, many patients visit the few existing practices. This leaves no time for therapists to familiarize themselves with new, less well-known health topics (e.g., autism).

I have severe limitations in my daily life; I can barely go shopping, can't hold a job long-term, and can't study, even though I'm intellectually above average. There are government-funded support programs for people with autism. However, you can only get them with a corresponding diagnosis.
Psychiatrists and psychotherapists refuse treatment as soon as they hear the word "autism."

The few specialists in the field of autism have a waiting time of up to two years and are very difficult for me to reach. I need a companion to attend appointments. Due to work commitments and family care needs, there is no one in my area who could accompany me. I can only receive state-funded support with a diagnosis.

According to German statistics, I now live in poverty. I know that I am, in principle, capable of leading a reasonably independent life, but I will need support and daily assistance for a while to achieve this independence. Even a severely disabled person's ID card would help me. But even for this, I have to present the relevant diagnoses and reports.

Conclusion:
More funds must be made available for psychiatric/psychological treatment services. Furthermore, the limit on the number of psychiatric/psychotherapeutic practices imposed by state health insurance companies must be lifted. Medical care must not be restricted! This should be more important than the auto and coal industries.

Older people mostly found the language repulsive and the condemnation of people who think differently it contained wrong. I still don't have health insurance, despite it supposedly being mandatory in Germany. I was fascinated by how difficult it is to get health insurance when you move here from abroad as a self-employed person. You'd think that founders in particular would be massively sought after as potential employers in Germany, but instead, the unspeakable bureaucracy and far too many levels of competency in every aspect make getting settled here incredibly difficult.

For example, the health insurance issue mentioned above. As a self-employed person, you're not required to have insurance, and if you're from abroad, even voluntary statutory insurance isn't that easy to obtain. So you think you'll get private insurance because it should be possible somehow. No way. You enter your information online, then you get a call from an insurance agent, with whom you have five meetings before you get to the risk department, where your information is interpreted differently, resulting in the denial of insurance. Then you ask whether the relevant condition can't simply be excluded. Then it goes back again and you wait and wait and you can't even get health insurance in this shitty country.

Young people aren't listened to when they talk about their concerns. This was true when I was a teenager, and it's still true today.
For example, I'm hearing from more and more young people that they're tired of being addicted to screen time. They know they're addicted, but they can't seem to break free. At the same time, the education system believes that schools must become increasingly digital. There's an online classroom for every subject, where assignments must be set and submitted, etc. Online tutoring is being pushed by tutoring institutes. The only thing young people aren't getting is a solid digital education. They don't want to spend so much time glued to screens, yet they're forced to. Who would have thought that 30 years ago, when people said young people weren't going outside anymore and were getting "square eyes" from television?
This is just one of hundreds of examples. Whether it's about education policy, mental health, or whatever, the concerns of young people are dismissed as inferior by adults—politicians and everyone else—or even ignored at all. What are young people supposed to know? They are being forced into a system by adults that oppresses them. This must finally stop.

column1: A very difficult situation. I was brought in as a service provider to  play a very small role in using complexity thinking to mediate the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The people who commissioned my services were Americans. On the call were Americas, Brits, Israelis and Palestinians. A Palestinian woman who was part of the process became enraged at the service we were providing yet was gracious enough to apologise to me afterwards. I felt sick thinking about how much space she holds for others even as a bulls-eye is painted on her back. I am a British woman of Irish descent. My great-grandmother had to hide in her back-garden from murderous British soldiers. My grandma who moved to England faced a lifetime of brutal prejudice. She had to live with the paradoxical decision of fleeing to the UK to escape the British occupation of Ireland. Her children and grandchildren are of course Brits. She tried to distance us from our Irish roots to gain us freedom.  For example she pretended she could not speak the Irish language even though she had to learn English as a second language as a child. This felt like a betrayal at first. I would ask her about a Gaelic word that she had carved on the house. She would say "I don't know." I later found out, after she had passed, that that word translated meant "freedom" in Gaelic. I couldn't understand why she wouldn't tell me. I'm technically still an EU citizen by virtue of my Irish roots though I haven't applied for the Irish passport to which I'm entitled yet. I'm somehow more acutely aware of my difference from other Brits and the prejudice I face post-Brexit. I remember The Guardian (supposedly a progressive newspaper) publishing a column commenting on every 'Tom, Mick and Paddy' applying for an Irish passport post-Brexit. This is a play on the British expression "Tom, Dick and Harry" meaning everyone (Thomas, Richard, Harry are very common English names) and the racial slur against the Irish ("Micks and Paddys" being a common slur.) Of course though that racism has always been there. I find the pro-european sentiment in my country uncomfortable post-Brexit. Are you asking me to identify with immigrants (I do)? Are you asking me to identify with people because they are white (I don't)? In the city where I live, people often sit on the street begging for money. I used to give them some small change every now and then. Until one day, my roommate told me he saw a woman being driven by a car to her "begging spot" early in the morning. column1:
My husband recently lost his driving licence temporarily due to a health condition and we lived in a small village in East Devon, England.  With me travelling away a lot, he suddenly experienced himself as being utterly cut off, and powerless to make choices for simple things like shopping.  Attempts to use public transport led to frustration and increased powerlessness, as there is no local train station and the buses are utterly unreliable, often not turning up at all, let alone on time.

He found himself having to ask neighbours for lifts (which he hated doing), and I experienced myself becoming more and more unwilling to accept work that kept me away from home for more than a day or two at best.  We felt our world closing in on us.

Ultimately, even though he got his licence back when the health issue was resolved, we decided to leave the village, and have now moved to central London - the opposite to what many people do at our age.  We have been surprised to find that local engagement and invitation to get to know others is BETTER here than it was in our Devon village, which we now realise was cliquey and hard to enter if you weren't born there, and didn't have school aged kids, or belong to a religious community.

What started as a transport problem, was actually more to do with becoming vulnerable in a community that we found it hard to engage with, and made little effort to engage us.  We are much happier in the "village in the city".

column1:
In my daily work, I work a lot with vulnerable people, such as (functionally) illiterate people, people with disabilities, and people whose native language isn't German. Therefore, I consciously avoid correct gender in writing and speech and use simple language. I ask myself what is actually inclusive? If identity excludes and divides more than it improves everyone's lives, I don't see the point.
Example: I'm often asked what I'm going to vote for—actually, Volt. The reactions are almost always the same. Environment and Europe, yes. But too much focus on identity. The LGBTQ+ issue, in particular, is perceived as too big in light of our current problems. Not because my conversation partners don't respect the rights of queer people, but because other issues are simply perceived as much more important. Around 10% of the vote is an attractive prospect, but at least that many might not vote for Volt because of it.
It would be great if Volt could also reach the LGBTQ+ community with issues that appeal to all citizens. People are unsettled. My experience is quite clear: people long for common ground.
The article on identity politics, published in HPD on January 13, 2025, is highly recommended: https://hpd.de/artikel/identitaetspolitiken-links-und-rechts-perfekte-sturm-22754

I've been working for a few months at a social enterprise in my city, completing an extracurricular internship.
However, I don't want to talk about my own experience (though it's also quite problematic), but rather that of the many student interns I've met.
I'm increasingly aware of how my fellow students, with curricular internship contracts (without a salary), are shamelessly exploited.
It's not just the lack of compensation for full-time commitment to the company (which is unacceptable in itself), but rather the system by which these people are deluded into believing they'll receive adequate job training and that this experience will open doors to the world of work, when in reality it's simply a way for companies to work for free...
Very often, internships are used when someone needs someone to perform a strenuous or uninspiring task and they don't want to pay an employee. Everything is out in the open, everything is explicitly stated: the curricular intern serves only to do the dirty work without paying.
Sometimes the "boss" doesn't even remember the names of the interns, who come and go at a dizzying pace and very rarely have truly formative relationships with their colleagues.
The cynicism with which these people are treated is intolerable; the purpose of internships should be fundamentally rethought, without exploiting the weakness of all those young people who know they are vulnerable in the contemporary world of work and who must submit to these unjust practices.

Mi rendo conto  infatti sempre più spesso di quanto i miei colleghi studenti, con contratto da tirocinante curriculare (senza stipendio) siano sfruttati senza alcun ritegno.
Non è solo la mancata erogazione di un compenso a fronte di un impegno lavorativo full time in azienda (cosa di per sé inaccettabile), quanto piuttosto il sistema per cui si illudono queste persone facendo loro credere che riceveranno una formazione al lavoro adeguata e che questa esperienza aprirà loro le porte del mondo del lavoro, quando si tratta solamente di un modo per dare alle aziende qualcuno che lavori gratis...
Molto spesso si ricorre ai tirocini quando si ha bisogno di qualcuno che svolga qualche mansione faticosa o poco stimolante e non si ha voglia di pagare un dipendente. Tutto alla luce del sole, tutto esplicitamente detto: il tirocinante curriculare serve solo a fare il lavoro sporco senza sborsare soldi.
A volte il "capo" nemmeno si ricorda il nome dei tirocinanti, che vanno e vengono ad un ritmo vertiginoso e molto raramente hanno davvero dei rapporti formativi con i colleghi.
Il cinismo con il quale questo persone vengono trattate e' intollerabile, andrebbe ripensata alla radice la funzione dei tirocini, senza approfittare della debolezza di tutti quei giovani che sanno di essere vulnerabili nel mondo del lavoro contemporaneo e che devono sottostare a queste pratiche ingiuste

I am very worried about the future of our democracy / democracies. The developments in the US offer a glimpse into the type of oligarchy, cronyism, and corruption that awaits us here in Europe as well. I feel that with social media and billionaires, Russia and China spreading misinformation and propaganda, all we can influence is our direct environment, people in our immediate communities. I am disheartened by the lack of willingness to engage, listen, accept other people's viewpoints. I understand how many people feel nobody is listening to them, and I would really like to help with that. When you listen to people, without judgment, they open up and like feeling heard. I just do not know how sustainable any of this is.
The specific experience: I ended up in hospital in Austria, and I shared my room with two women I would never have met in my normal life. Both voted for the FPÖ (far right) in the last elections. These were the first people I have ever met who said they voted for that party, and I was a little shocked. They were nice, reasonable, friendly women who tried to make their lives work and who were concerned about the state of the country. They felt that nobody is interested in them and nobody would listen anyway. I did not start fights with them, I just listened and let them explain to me what they thought was the point in elections, in voting for the FPÖ, how they did not take the racism (and homophobia etc.) too seriously, how they felt they had no other choice. It opened my eyes to see they were compassionate and intelligent people and not the dumb racist nazis I had expected these voters to be. I will not vote far right ever, but I know better than to demonise the people we can still reach.

column1:
A few years ago, I moved within Germany from a western state to an eastern one. There, I'm constantly being pressured to account for my origins, my living conditions, why I'm moving there, what I want there, and why I don't go somewhere else. In the process, I'm repeatedly subjected to false accusations, insults, threats, and sexism, all by locals and almost exclusively by older people, around 50 years and older. When I then realize what they think of me and what they're threatening me with, it always hits me like an electric shock. I'll just pick one incident with a neighbor as an example:

A neighbor, initially relatively friendly, arranged to meet me. She talked about herself, laughed about my birthday on "Walpurgis Night" on April 30th, and listened to me. Until, after a few months, she began making anti-Semitic statements about me in a friendly, narrative tone: My clothes were missing a "brooch," two triangles, and preferably in sunflower yellow. Or she repeatedly recommended that I walk as far as possible along the paths behind the houses at the edge of the settlement. She thought they were perfect for me, especially in spring; regardless of whether I went left or right, I would definitely find what I experienced there the absolute and highest point of my life. I thought of beautiful nature and viewpoints until I realized she meant the Nazi routes used to evacuate the camps in April 1945. To the left led to the labor camps, and to the right led to the brutal, often deadly marches across the Harz Mountains. There are more such examples. I try to avoid her these days, to keep my physical distance from her.

But after the turn of the year, I had something to do at the post office on my very first day of work. We stood one behind the other in the queue. She had a bad cold, looked gray and ill. I was simply polite, greeted her, and automatically wished her a Happy New Year. She sneezed and sniffed and replied that her current information wasn't so good that she was still hoping for something good. I asked if it was because of the cold. Afterwards, I wanted to go to the pharmacy myself and offered to pick up some medicine. She replied, "Why pharmacy? You're still here."

Wenn ich dann begreife, was die von mir denken und womit die mir drohen, trifft es mich jedes Mal wie ein Stromschlag. Ich picke hier nur mal eine Episode mit einer Nachbarin als Beispiel heraus:

Eine Nachbarin, zeigte sich anfangs vergleichsweise freundlich, verabredete sich mit mir. Sie erzählte von sich, lachte über meinen Geburtstag in der "Walpurgisnacht" am 30. April  und hörte mir zu.  Bis sie nach einigen Monaten anfing in freundlichem Erzählton antisemitische Aussagen über mich zu machen: An meiner Kleidung fehle eine "Brosche", zwei Dreiecke und die am Besten in Sonnenblumengelb. Oder sie empfahl mir mehrfach, die Wege hinter den Häusern am Rande der Siedlung möglichst weit entlangzuwandern. Die fände sie besonders im Frühling genau passend für mich, egal ob ich nach links oder rechts gehen würde, was ich da erlebe, fände ich bestimmt das Absolute und Höchste in meinem Leben. Ich dachte an schöne Natur und Aussichtspunkte, bis ich herausfand, daß sie die Nazi-Routen zur Räumung der Lager im April 1945 meinte. Nach links ging es zu den Arbeitslagern und nach rechts führten die brutalen oft tödlichen Märsche über den Harz. Es gibt noch mehr solcher Beispiele. Ich versuche sie inzwischen zu meiden, räumliche Distanz zu ihr zu halten.

column1:
A story for you at Volt

1977: the birth of Mother's Scents flower incense.

Empowerment, a job, safety, and hope for women, before the term even existed.

In 1977, there were no jobs for women. The only work women could do was housework.
A woman was no longer allowed to work after marriage (as was the case in the Netherlands long ago).
At our studio, their husbands often allowed them to continue working because we consider it safe for women.
And with us, women gained hope for a better life, especially for their children.

And our incense was organic, hand-rolled, and sustainable.
All incense sticks in India were rolled scentless at home, and later the sticks were dipped in a factory (the dipping method) in an incense oil diluted up to 7 to 10 times with phthalates, which are now banned due to hormone disruptions.

With our incense, the frankincense oil isn't diluted, but used directly in the incense dough (the masala method). Therefore, the incense can't be rolled at home, but only under supervision in a workshop. This explains the jobs created for women. When I had to leave, there were around 200 women working there.

Now, for reasons of affordability, almost all incense in India is rolled by machine. Depending on the size, a machine can take over the rolling of 50 to 200 women.

However, we continue to roll by hand.

An interesting fact is that the incense packaging is made of hand-marbled paper, making each package unique since 1977: a unique gift made by women.

1977: de geboorte van de Moeder’s Geuren bloemenwierook.

Empowerment, een baan, veiligheid en hoop voor vrouwen, avant la lettre.

In 1977 waren er geen banen voor vrouwen. Er was voor een vrouw alleen werk in de huishouding. 
Een vrouw mocht na haar trouwen niet meer werken (zoals heel vroeger in Nederland).
Bij ons atelier mochten ze vaak van hun man blijven werken omdat het bij ons vrouw-veilig is.
En bij ons kregen de vrouwen hoop op een beter bestaan, vooral voor hun kinderen.

En onze wierook was biologisch, handgerold en duurzaam.
Alle wierooksoorten in India werden geurloos thuis gerold en later werden de stokjes in een fabriek gedipt (de dip methode) in een wierookolie verdund tot zelfs 7 tot 10 keer met ftalaten, die nu verboden zijn vanwege hormoonverstoringen. 
Bij onze wierook wordt de wierookolie niet verdund, maar direct in het wierookdeeg gebruikt (de masala methode). De wierook kan daarom niet thuis gerold worden en alleen onder toezicht in een atelier. Vandaar de banen die voor vrouwen gecreëerd werden. Toen ik moest vertrekken werkten er rond de 200 vrouwen. 
Nu wordt in India vrijwel alle wierook, vanwege goedkoopte, met een machine ‘gerold’. Een machine, afhankelijk van de grootte, kan het rollen overnemen van 50 tot 200 vrouwen. 
Wij blijven echter met de hand rollen. 

Een leuk weetje is dat de verpakking van de wierook bestaat uit handgemarmerd papier, waardoor elk pakje sinds 1977 uniek is: een uniek cadeau gemaakt door vrouwen.

column1:
I recently experienced how inefficient and bureaucratic our higher education system is. I speak from my own experience in higher education, as a lecturer at two completely different universities of applied sciences. Coming from the field, I see how seemingly intangible, inefficient, and unfortunately, not prioritizing the interests of society, things are.

Coming from the field myself, I see that within higher education, it seems more about procedures, structure, and the knowledge of textbook authors than about the useful knowledge from science and practice. Consider also lessons learned, etc.
Universities of applied sciences assess each other to ensure quality. The organizations for which students are trained play only a marginal role.

The system creates its own reality. Once the process is followed, the outcome is no longer open to question. A practical example is that student connection should stem from strict classroom rules, something they proclaim with a straight face. Structure trumps passion for the student.
And, for example, the hype focused on "skills." The skill of "collaboration" means that almost all assessments are group work. Important, but to put it mildly: it's a quick way to mark things. And the students don't collaborate; they simply divide the tasks among themselves.

The higher professional education system isn't useless, but it could be much, much more efficient.

A concrete example of improvement:
Internships in Business Administration are only offered in the second year, if the student is lucky. At the AUAS (University of Applied Sciences) this is still being investigated, as they don't require them until the third year. And yet all my colleagues agree that students only understand what we teach after an internship, and that afterward, students show much more interest and "grab" it.

I advocate for simultaneous internships and theory courses. Starting in the first year. And then a different internship every few months, in as diverse an organization as possible.
Advantages:
- Direct connection with practice, instead of something my colleagues devised with a distance to practice. - In classrooms, the exchange takes place based on the latest insights
- Students contribute to society earlier
- Students know years earlier what they want after their studies, what suits them
- Students understand what they are studying for; this motivates: more attention from the student, a faster learning curve, better understanding, and a much lower dropout rate in the first two years, which now affects half (!) of all students.

In short, quality and enjoyment are up, and costs are down!

Another example: student numbers are declining sharply, new lecturers are not being hired, yet Windesheim Almere is about to build a new building in the center of Almere. In all honesty, this serves egos and not the public interest. It costs money that doesn't go to education itself.

I grew up in an entrepreneurial family, studied law from the age of 15, and subsequently worked for small and very large organizations. A few years ago, I became a lecturer at the HBO Business Administration program. First at a small and more recently at a very large HBO program.

Afkomstig uit de praktijk zie ik hoe schijnbaar ongrijpbaar inefficient en helaas ook niet in met het maatschappelijk belang voorop het er aan toe gaat.

Ik kom zelf uit de praktijk en zie dat het binnen het HBO meer om procedures , structuur en kennis van schrijvers van lesboeken lijkt te gaan dan de nuttige kennis uit de wetenschap en praktijk. Denk ook aan lessons learned e.d. 
HBO's beoordelen elkaar om zo de kwaliteit te borgen. De organisaties waarvoor wordt opgeleid spelen maar een marginale rol. 

Het systeem creëert een eigen werkelijkheid. Als het proces gevolgd is, staat de uitkomst niet meer ter discussie. Een praktisch voorbeeld is dat de binding met student zou moeten komen uit strenge regels in de klas, wat met droge ogen wordt verkondigd. De structuur wint het van de passie voor de student.
En zoals bijvoorbeeld de hype gericht op 'vaardigheden'. De vaardigheid 'samenwerken' maakt dat bijna alle toetsing groepswerk is. Belangrijk, maar flauw gezegd: het is lekker snel nakijken. En de student werkt niet samen, maar men verdeelt alleen onderling de taken.

Het HBO systeem is niet nutteloos, maar het kan veel, veel efficiënter. 

Een concreet verbetervoorbeeld: 
Stage bij Bedrijfskunde is er pas in jaar 2, als de student geluk heeft. Bij de HvA is dat iets wat nog onderzocht wordt, want daar is dat pas verplicht in jaar 3. En dat terwijl al mijn collega's het erover eens zijn dat de studenten pas na stage begrijpen wat we als docent onderwijzen en dat studenten daarna veel meer interesse tonen en het 'pakken'.

Ik pleit voor gelijktijdige stage en theorie. Vanaf het eerste jaar. En dan iedere paar maanden een andere stage, in een zo verschillend mogelijke organisatie.
voordelen: 
- directe koppeling met praktijk, ipv bedacht door mijn collega's met afstand tot de praktijk.
- in klaslokalen vind de uitwisseling plaats op basis van de nieuwste inzichten
- studenten dragen al eerder bij een de maatschappij
- studenten weten jaren eerder wat ze willen na hun studie, wat er bij ze past
- studenten begrijpen waar ze voor leren; dit motiveert: meer aandacht van de student, sneller leercurve, beter begrip en veel minder uitval in de eerste twee jaar, wat nu de helft (!) van de studenten betreft.

Kortom kwaliteit en plezier omhoog en kosten omlaag!

Nog een voorbeeld: de student aantallen lopen fors terug, nieuwe docenten worden niet aangenomen, maar Windesheim Almere staat op het punt nieuwbouw te gaan plegen in het centrum van Almere. Dat dient in alle eerlijkheid ego's en niet het maatschappelijk belang. Dat kost geld dat niet naar het onderwijs zelf gaat.

In fact, I once registered (or had registered) the domains internetkamer.nl and derdekamer.nl.

1. Every decision we can vote on has so many consequences that the average Dutch person can't foresee them. So it's very difficult for a non-expert to take a position on this and can easily lead to unintended 'collateral damage'; after all, we don't send our best people to vote for us for nothing!

Volt has decided to abandon X.

I'm really struggling with this X decision...
Initially: "Yes, boycott that X!"
It's become a bizarre platform, and Facebook is going after it...

At the same time,
a. Do we really want everyone to retreat to their own platform to only hear what they want?
b. Who will then voice their dissent? A different perspective on the matter for the millions who do stick around?
c. MM's current framing/observation is that the left-wing elite really doesn't understand what's going on among ordinary citizens. Retreating to their own platform confirms that impression and makes understanding each other even more difficult (a bit like an 'American situation' with two opposing parties).
d. We Volts, as true democrats, pride ourselves on freedom of speech. So why be critical of a platform that facilitates it?
e. Not fact-checking: is that bad? I think so, but/however... who checks the fact-checker? State media agents? "Independent" (unknown?) journalists/experts? Who then?

So I'm unsure which is better.

In any case, even though I wholeheartedly support leaving X, my mind tells me it will further polarization, reduce dissent, and increase disparities.
Moreover, the reach of new Volt posts has been SIGNIFICANTLY reduced (thus fewer potential new members), and it primarily targets like-minded individuals who we don't need to incorporate into our vision for the world anyway!

Having fled the city shortly after my retirement, I took refuge in a corner of the countryside. 6,000 liters of rainwater irrigate my toilets and my land when drought strikes. Photovoltaic panels sit atop the roofs.
I leave my few acres of garden fallow and reintroduce plant species native to my region. I buy my dairy products from a nearby farm. I have local produce delivered.
Over the course of my life, I've seen major retailers gradually kill off local commerce, the kind that built society. Today, they play the violin in the ears of consumers who are tired of their credo: "economies of scale." They've started mimicking the neighborhood grocery store they banished decades earlier. It's a deception. A single religion prevails: profit. Price has become the sole selling point, to the detriment of quality, sustainability, and health. Producers are being strangled.
I'm doing my part, but it seems tiny compared to what needs to be done to return to a minimum of humanity and social cohesion.
Europe must be united or risk being crushed. But it must be united around more regionalized projects. We can move mountains with social cohesion. The neoliberalism that drives globalization is destroying the bond and the very essence of humanity.
Volt interests me because of the cross-border aspect, and I also like to hear that you have an approach that respects regional specificities.
People who are losing their identity and see the far right as a way out frighten me. What level of deprivation of freedoms and cultural mortification are they capable of adhering to? The duty of remembrance is no longer enough. We must highlight all the human rights violations that accompany dictatorships. The United States is showing us the wrong path... Have we failed? Are our children no longer being raised in the spirit of enlightenment? Is it the digital tidal wave that is destroying the very engine of our democracies: contradictory analysis?
Is it possible to rediscover values ​​other than the sole pursuit of profit? Have we forgotten to this extent that we are mortal and that the accumulation of goods is futile as long as we can house, feed, clothe, and heat ourselves?
Can we still count on the political world to stop climate change? Citizen mobilization seems more convincing today. If we can no longer influence decision-makers, we must act at the Achilles' heel: consumption, which fuels the power of those who are acquiring more and more monopolies. Do we want to boost an economy? How can favoring large companies and monopolies encourage entrepreneurship? Does creating startups prevent them from ending up being sold to large corporations that then swallow them up to become ever more powerful?
I grew up with the mantra: "the economy regulates itself through the principle of supply and demand"... This is no longer very relevant. If we allow a company to become a behemoth that takes all the market share, where is the self-regulation? More SMEs competing with each other—isn't that what boosts the economy?

J'ai vu au cours de ma vie les grands distributeurs tuer, pied à pied, le commerce local, celui qui faisait société. Aujourd'hui, ils jouent du violon aux oreilles des consommateurs qui sont fatigués de leur credo: "l'économie d'échelle". Ils se mettent à mimer l'épicerie de quartier qu'ils avaient bannie quelques décennies plus tôt. C'est un leurre. Une seule religion prévaut: le profit. Le prix est devenu l'unique argument de vente au détriment de la qualité, de la durabilité, de la santé. Les producteurs sont étranglés.
Je fais ma part, mais ça me paraît infime à côté de ce qu'il y a à faire pour retourner à un minimum d'humanité et de lien social.
L'Europe doit être unie sous peine de se faire écraser. Mais elle doit doit être unie autour de projets plus régionalisés. On déplace des montagnes avec de la cohésion sociale. Le néolibéralisme qui conduit la mondialisation détruit le lien et l'essence-même de l'humanité.
Volt m'intéresse par l'aspect transfrontalier et j'aime aussi entendre que vous avez une approche qui respecte les spécificités régionales. 
Les gens en perte d'identité qui voient en l'extrême-droite une porte de sortie m'effraient. A quel niveau de privation de libertés, de mortifications de la culture  sont-ils capables d'adhérer? Le devoir de mémoire ne suffit plus. Il faut relever toutes les atteintes aux droits de l'homme qui vont avec les dictatures. Les USA nous montrent la voie à ne pas suivre... Avons-nous failli? Est-il possible de retrouver d'autres valeurs que la seule recherche de profit? Avons-nous, à ce point, oublié que nous sommes mortels et que l'accumulation de biens est vaine dès lors que nous pouvons nous loger, nous nourrir, nous vêtir, nous chauffer.
Peut-on encore compter sur le monde politique pour enrayer le dérèglement climatique? La mobilisation citoyenne semble aujourd’hui plus convaincante. Every 3rd year I have been able to vote in a municipality or county council/regional election but ...... never in the parliamentary election! I consider this to be a major shortcoming in today's EU, which among other things gives us EUR citizens the right to stay and work in another EU country. When we moved, we were therefore not able to take our democratic rights with us and thus could not elect politicians who would be able to bring our case to the political body that decides, among other things, how our tax money is used. As an EU citizen, you should not have to become (in our case) a Swedish citizen and thereby (in our case) renounce your Dutch citizenship in order to fully participate in all democratic elections in the EU country where you live, work and pay taxes.

Some time ago, I became aware of an uncontrolled, i.e. illegal, garbage dump in a somewhat remote location in my area (southern Greece). It was clearly professionally constructed, with a specially constructed concrete loading ramp. A friend and I tried to get clarification from the local community. A wall of silence: "We don't know anything about it." A newspaper article only led to comments along the lines of: What does the foreigner want here? A complaint to the EU in Brussels also yielded nothing: "We've asked the relevant authorities to take care of it..." There were no attempts from any side to remove these hundreds of tons of garbage, which also threaten a beach during heavy rains. "No money."
Then there was another citizen action: a protest against a planned wind farm in the mountains. In a nature reserve (where the garbage dump is also located, by the way), a petition suddenly garnered thousands of signatures to prevent the "destruction of the environment."
My conclusion: When it comes to something that could potentially affect someone locally financially, everyone stays silent. When someone from outside comes along who wants to implement a profitable project, everyone is loudly against it.

column1:
My daughter has a developmental delay in cognitive and physical abilities due to a congenital brain malformation. She is currently in the first grade of a regular school. There, she is one of many children with special needs. In our opinion, this inclusive education is the best solution for our daughter, as it gives her the opportunity to reach her full potential, which is always difficult to determine in children with special needs (especially "GE" children = intellectual development). Many GE children therefore go to a special needs center and are educated separately from healthy children. On the one hand, this ensures that some of the potential of affected children is never developed and they remain under-challenged, which reduces their future prospects. On the other hand, it reinforces the German practice of placing an above-average number of children in special schools.
In our daughter's case, however, the path to our desired school was a major challenge, as there are various bodies that influence the allocation of school places: the school authority, the youth welfare office, schools, possibly special needs centers or assessing bodies, etc.
As always, it ultimately comes down to suitability and availability. Unfortunately, this is the real problem: too few schools have the appropriate staffing and infrastructure to accept students, as well as the necessary experience. However, demand is far greater than supply. I advocate for more positions for special education teachers in schools, along with more school support staff. Also, easier ways for schools to implement or commission measures to create accessibility (see building regulations).

Meine Tochter ist aufgrund einer angeborenen Hirnfehlbildung entwicklungsverzögert in Bezug auf kognitive und physische Leistungsfähigkeit. Sie geht aktuell in die 1. Klasse einer Regelschule. Dort ist sie eines von zahlreichen Kindern mit Förderschwerpunkt. Diese inklusive Beschulung ist aus unserer Sicht für unsere Tochter die beste Lösung, da sie ihr die Möglichkeit gibt, ihr volle Potenzial auszuschöpfen, was bei Kindern mit Förderschwerpunkt (besonders bei „GE“-Kindern = geistige Entwicklung) immer schwer zu ermitteln ist. Viele GE Kinder gehen daher in ein Förderzentrum und werden getrennt von gesunden Kindern beschult. Das sorgt zum einen dafür, dass manche Potentiale betroffener Kinder niemals gefördert werden und sie stets unterfordert bleiben, was ihre Zukunftschancen mindert. Zum Anderen verfestigt es die deutsche Praxis, überdurchschnittlich viele Kinder in Sonderschulen zu betreuen. 
Im Falle unserer Tochter war der Weg jedoch in unsere Wunschschule eine große Herausforderung, da es verschiedene Stellen gibt, die die Schulplatzvergabe mit beeinflussen: Schulamt, Jugendamt, Schulen, ggf. SPZs bzw. begutachtende Stellen usw. 
Wie immer kommt es am Ende auf Geeignetheit und Verfügbarkeit an. Hier liegt leider das eigentliche Problem: zu wenige Schulen haben entsprechende personelle und infrastrukturelle Ausstattungen sowie die notwendige Erfahrung Schülerinnen und Schüler aufzunehmen. Hier ist aber die Nachfrage viel größer als das Angebot. Mein Plädoyer für mehr Stellen für Sonderpädagoginnen/-Pädagogen in den Schulen in Verbindung mit mehr Schulhelfern. Auch einfachere Möglichkeiten für Schulen, Maßnahmen zur Schaffung von Barrierefreiheit durchzuführen bzw. zu beauftragen (siehe Bauordnung).

I haven’t a recent experience of me in our society, unless personal ideas development, retractions from politics due to lack of will and power concentration from elected officers, far right French MP and many people in the Boulogne-sur-Mer area. Being candidate for Regional in 2021 wasn’t easy at all, facing how citizens were pretty disgusted. Too many critics or pretexts about our community places for poor results from them. Boulogne, a town dead. That’s all they’re able to say without reconsider our potential and open their minds to the world we are building.

Boulogne-sur-Mer area is underrated, concentrated to fish industry and Nausicaá whilst it has the potential to be a better and powerful place between London and Brussels.  The town and its areas suffered from wars, the French State and local officers have no will to make it richer and rethink its attractiveness. I’m really concerned about the place I live as personal and as visitor. When I travel elsewhere in Europe and the UK, It feels like you’ve find your way back to the world of civilization after being lost in the forest. 

Since always, Europe makes sense for a lot of things and although the National Rally (Antoine Golliot and Christine Engrand) won Boulonnais constituencies in 2024, Europe is important for the prosperity and the well-being of the Boulonnais people. 

Under the French centralism rule, our territory cannot express itself with its lack of emancipation because it’s considered as a territory in the North of Paris rather than in the heart of Europe.

To make our territory “Great Again” in a better way than our lil’bro USA, it needs to be more autonomous, sharing a special status within France and the EU at the same time, based on examples such as Åland, an associated-state with Finland. The main idea is to make the Boulonnais an European Laboratory for experiencing both EU and French public policies, close to the UK Post-Brexit. 

Thanks to the Autonomy, and the ability to have a wide and full competencies, with legislative bodies, we’ll be able to help our people and inspire others that EU works by having power to legislate, handle refugees crisis with more humanity, responds to floods, diversifying our economies through AI or decarbonization researches and develop Free trade zone to enhance our bound with Britain and Benelux, better transportation system with our neigbors, recognize Boulonnais/Picard , Dutch, English and French at the same level and not only French as sole language and Boulonnais/Picard as wrong French... Why not having an extended welfare system and more democracy, flex security inspired by other european countries.

That idea came a long time ago with aim to make Boulogne and the Boulonnais a better place to live in the 21st century, respond to crisis with neighbors, EU and State and set one step further to the foundation of the United States of Europe and perhaps, the Boulonnais will not become member, but just European State.

column1: I was active in Volt for over three years starting in 2020, but in 2024 I left. Not because I no longer believe in or stand for what Volt was founded on. In the beginning, it was very simple: Justice, Equality, Sustainability, and Solidarity, and you can't achieve that alone, at least at the European level. It started so well, and now we're represented at all levels. The reason I left is simple: the same behavior I so condemn has become acceptable within Volt. The way Nilufer's departure was handled, the way we blindly follow parties in the municipalities where we participate that systematically exclude others, and the way we abuse democratic rights to justify inexcusable behavior. How we want to elevate exceptions to the rule. Democracy isn't a right; you have to earn it and, unfortunately, sometimes even fight for it. Claiming it but not standing up for the rights of those who think differently doesn't create tolerance but rather further divides people. Don't get me wrong, I still support the pillars on which Volt is built, but we're taking the wrong turn. I see Volt increasingly focusing on treating the symptoms instead of addressing the root causes. A positive exception is their stance on defense; unfortunately, a powerful military apparatus is necessary. But if you want to do something about the climate, you have to address the root cause: the 120 million people in China living in poverty, or child poverty in general. While our well-educated children are driving down the highway, according to UNICEF, 300 million children still live in extreme poverty. What argument should I use to deny these people the opportunity to try to escape that poverty? And then there's the women's quota. I'd love to see more women in politics, but in today's world, driven by social media and big data and governed by men who have little regard for equality, you see the opposite. Driven by what algorithms deliver, women are becoming more left-leaning and men more right-leaning. So don't limit yourself by ideals. If there are men who are willing and able to contribute what we need women for in politics, then take advantage of that. Don't confuse the goal with the means. Men and women are not equal, and that's precisely the beauty of it. Not everyone feels comfortable in a male or female box, and that's okay, but we're not all the same, and that's precisely the beauty of it. And what about equality? That too is very simple: you are only equal if you accept others as equals. Equality doesn't mean that everyone has to think or feel what you feel.

I'm 65 years old and have spent over 40 years in healthcare: after completing my medical studies, I did alternative military service at an institution for people with intellectual disabilities. Afterward, I specialized as a rehabilitation physician, and in that role, I've worked for over 30 years, working with patients and rehabilitation teams, as a trainer and researcher, mostly in the practice. I recently retired.

I'm happy and healthy. "All my basic needs are met," such as housing, family, hobbies, and so on. A good retirement. "What more could you want?" Almost everyone tells me: "Enjoy it now!" Sure; well-intentioned, and I enjoy it, but still... I don't need a camper van with bicycles on the back. I'm not going on a world trip. I hope to live a few more years and am now "available" to others in a new way. For example, I teach. And I care for my grandchildren. My repertoire as an amateur pianist is steadily growing.

However, how do we, in our society, make good (preferably optimal, of course) use of the potential of people who are not (or no longer) active in their original profession (in my case, that of a practicing physician)? column1: I've been talking to some people for a while now about the "network of networks"—that is, a level at which all relevant groups and actors become visible, but above all, effective, across regions. column1:
Growing up in the northeastern United States, my town (like many in New England at the time) operated hyper-democratically with an annual Town Meeting. All of the town's citizens gathered each year to act as the town's legislative body, debating and making policy decisions.

One of my earliest memories of our Town Meeting had us debating the extension of a regional highway system through our town. I was young, so my perceptions of it at the time were of lots of very opinionated adults being very loud and the discussion being very boring. Now though, a few decades later, it's rather impactful in that day's decisions continues to shape the regional transportation infrastructure... We decided not to allow the highway to pass through the town, and so the highway (Route 25) exists only from the coast through the nearest city, where it abruptly ends and forces you to take local roads until connecting with the next highway a few towns later.

It's impactful to me in the level of long-term power and impact given to a very citizen-level process, while also (again in retrospect) demonstrating some challenges to regional cooperation in a democratic framework.

I live on a European internal border (Germany/Netherlands) and therefore travel by public transport on both sides. Thanks to an EU project, a train now crosses the border here, but the connection is very unreliable because the two systems are incompatible, meaning each section is always operated by a local crew. Especially on the German part of the route, disruptions due to staff shortages are extremely common. I also need a separate app with a separate account for each mobility provider. Compatibility is usually non-existent, especially across the border, which I find very regrettable. For climate protection reasons, it is extremely important to me to use public transport, even if it sometimes takes considerably longer.
Nevertheless, I greatly enjoy the opportunity to visit neighboring cities without having to exchange currency, etc. I am convinced that better connections across borders will bring Europe closer together.
